original_summary: Decrypto is a team word-deduction game. Each team holds four secret keywords. Each round an Encryptor gives three meaning-based clues for a secret 3-digit code. Teammates try to decode it while the opponents try to intercept it from the growing public clue history. Two Interceptions win and two Miscommunications lose.

review.evidence: No simple policy wins. A fixed decode guess is right 1/24 of the time and loses by about the second encryption. A fixed intercept hits 1/24 and almost never reaches 2. The always-obvious clue is decoded but becomes interceptable as history builds. The previous variation, however, ran the end check after every single round, with Team A always encrypting first. Equal-pace races then resolved against A: about 53.5% against 46.5%, a 7-point seat edge for B. The original Decrypto avoids this by resolving both teams in the same round before checking.

Results are driven by skill. Good clues must be clear to a partner who shares the keywords, yet vague to an opponent who sees only the history. Good interceptors cross-reference past clues per column. The random code only fixes which digits are clued and does not favour either team.
Clue calibration against a growing public history has no ceiling. A weak team still decodes most of its own codes and can win on the opponent's mistakes.
Interceptors infer hidden keywords from scattered clues. Encryptors model what the opponent can already infer and plan clue choices across rounds.
Code matches are exact digit comparisons and the tokens are public counts. Only clue validity goes to the referee, which the platform allows.

The step, attribute, hidden-element and draw counts are within limits, and the game is text-only and turn-based. The previous variation's Interceptor list contradicted its own stated rule in half the rounds, so a model could not tell who intercepts. It also announced Interceptors in rounds 1 and 2, when none exist.

problems: Seat edge: the end check ran after every round while Team A always encrypted first. Equal-pace failure races therefore went against A, giving B about a 7-point advantage.
Second-mover information edge: within any fixed pairing, the team that encrypts second sees the other team's result first and can adjust its risk.
Ambiguous roles: the Interceptor definition and the Interceptor list disagreed in rounds 5-8 and 13-16.
Minor: the round announcement named Interceptors in rounds 1-2, where interception does not happen.
The rules claimed that win conditions cannot conflict. Once checks are done per pair this claim is false, and no rule covered both teams triggering a win together.

changes.what: Group rounds into pairs (rounds 1-2, 3-4, ... 15-16) in which each team encrypts once. Run the end check only after the second round of each pair.
changes.why: Both teams then have the same number of encryptions and interception chances before any win or loss is checked. This restores the original's same-round symmetry.
changes.fixes: Seat edge: the end check ran after every round while Team A always encrypted first. Equal-pace failure races therefore went against A, giving B about a 7-point advantage.

changes.what: Alternate which team encrypts first in a pair: Team A in odd pairs, Team B in even pairs.
changes.why: Each team is the second mover equally often, so neither team gets the information edge more often.
changes.fixes: Second-mover information edge: within any fixed pairing, the team that encrypts second sees the other team's result first and can adjust its risk.

changes.what: Replace the Interceptor rule with fixed per-pair roles. In each pair, each team has one Encryptor and one Guesser. The Guesser decodes their own team's code and intercepts the other team's. Odd pairs: A1 and B1 encrypt. Even pairs: A2 and B2 encrypt. A full table is given.
changes.why: This gives one simple rule, stated both as a principle and as a table that agree. Every player has a role in every pair.
changes.fixes: Ambiguous roles: the Interceptor definition and the Interceptor list disagreed in rounds 5-8 and 13-16.

changes.what: The announcement in rounds 1-2 names the Encryptor and Decoder only, and states that there is no interception.
changes.why: This removes the contradiction between the announcement and the interception rule.
changes.fixes: Minor: the round announcement named Interceptors in rounds 1-2, where interception does not happen.

changes.what: Define that a team 'triggers' when it has 2 or more Interceptions, or when the other team has 2 or more Miscommunications. If exactly one team triggers at a pair check, it wins. If both trigger, the team with the higher Interceptions minus Miscommunications wins, and equal values are a draw.
changes.why: This handles simultaneous triggers arithmetically and removes the false claim.
changes.fixes: The rules claimed that win conditions cannot conflict. Once checks are done per pair this claim is false, and no rule covered both teams triggering a win together.

keeps: Two teams with four secret numbered keywords each.
A random 3-digit code of different digits 1-4, clued by meaning.
A public clue history per keyword column, which makes interception possible over time.
Two Interceptions win and two Miscommunications lose.
Encryptors rotate within a team, and there is no interception in the first round of each team.
Clues are the only communication channel.

recommendation.reason: The core deduction loop is strong and fits the limits. Only the turn order, the role table and the tie handling needed repair.

variation.name: Decrypto Duel (Paired Rounds)
variation.summary: Two teams of two run a 4-keyword Decrypto. Rounds are grouped into pairs in which each team encrypts once, and the first mover alternates between pairs. Wins and losses are checked only at the end of a pair, so neither seat has an edge.
variation.rules:
SETUP
- There are 4 players: Team A (A1, A2) and Team B (B1, B2).
- The engine deals each team 4 different keywords from a fixed list of 120 common concrete nouns. No word is given to both teams.
- A team's keywords are numbered 1 to 4. They are shown privately to both members of that team and never to the other team.
- A public clue history shows, for each team, four columns (keywords 1-4) that start empty.
- Each team starts with 0 Interceptions and 0 Miscommunications. Token counts are always public.

PAIRS AND ROLES
- The game has up to 16 rounds, grouped into 8 pairs: pair 1 = rounds 1-2, pair 2 = rounds 3-4, ..., pair 8 = rounds 15-16.
- In each pair, each team encrypts exactly once.
- In odd pairs (1, 3, 5, 7), Team A encrypts in the first round of the pair and Team B in the second.
- In even pairs (2, 4, 6, 8), Team B encrypts first and Team A second.
- In each pair, each team has one Encryptor and one Guesser:
  - Odd pairs: A1 and B1 are Encryptors; A2 and B2 are Guessers.
  - Even pairs: A2 and B2 are Encryptors; A1 and B1 are Guessers.
- In a round where a team encrypts:
  - The Encryptor is that team's Encryptor for the pair.
  - The Decoder is that team's Guesser.
  - The Interceptor is the other team's Guesser.
  - The other team's Encryptor only watches.
- Full table (round: Encryptor / Decoder / Interceptor):
  - R1: A1 / A2 / none
  - R2: B1 / B2 / none
  - R3: B2 / B1 / A1
  - R4: A2 / A1 / B1
  - R5: A1 / A2 / B2
  - R6: B1 / B2 / A2
  - R7: B2 / B1 / A1
  - R8: A2 / A1 / B1
  - R9: A1 / A2 / B2
  - R10: B1 / B2 / A2
  - R11: B2 / B1 / A1
  - R12: A2 / A1 / B1
  - R13: A1 / A2 / B2
  - R14: B1 / B2 / A2
  - R15: B2 / B1 / A1
  - R16: A2 / A1 / B1

EACH ROUND
1. The engine announces the round number, the encrypting team, the Encryptor and the Decoder. In rounds 3-16 it also announces the Interceptor. In rounds 1 and 2 it announces that there is no interception.
2. The engine draws a code uniformly at random from the 24 ordered sequences of three different digits from 1 to 4 (for example 3-1-4). It shows the code privately to the Encryptor only.
3. The Encryptor writes three clues, one per digit, in code order. Each clue points to the keyword with that number and is at most 3 words.
4. Referee check. The clue set is valid only if all of these hold:
   - Every clue relates to its keyword by meaning or association.
   - No clue hints by spelling, letters, letter count, rhyme, or keyword number or position.
   - No clue contains its keyword or a form of it.
   - No clue repeats any clue this team has used before.
   If the set is invalid:
   - The code is revealed to everyone.
   - The encrypting team gains 1 Miscommunication.
   - The clues are not added to the history.
   - The round goes to step 8.
5. The valid clues are shown to all players.
6. At the same moment, the Decoder privately submits a guessed 3-digit code and the Interceptor (if any) privately submits a guessed 3-digit code.
7. The true code and the guesses are revealed, then scored:
   - If the Decoder's guess differs from the true code in any digit, the encrypting team gains 1 Miscommunication.
   - If the Interceptor's guess equals the true code exactly, the Interceptor's team gains 1 Interception.
   - Each clue is added to the encrypting team's public history column for the keyword it clued.
8. End check, only in even-numbered rounds (the end of a pair). In odd-numbered rounds, play continues.
   - A team TRIGGERS if it has 2 or more Interceptions, or if the other team has 2 or more Miscommunications.
   - If exactly one team triggers, it wins and the game ends.
   - If both teams trigger, apply the comparison rule and the game ends.
   - If neither team triggers and this was round 16, apply the comparison rule.
   - Otherwise play continues.

COMPARISON RULE
- Each team's value is its Interceptions minus its Miscommunications.
- The higher value wins. Equal values are a draw.

COMMUNICATION
- There is no talk phase. Players communicate only through clues. Teammates may not message each other.
variation.objective: The winner is decided only at the end of an even-numbered round. A team triggers if it holds 2 or more Interceptions or if the opponent holds 2 or more Miscommunications. If exactly one team triggers, it wins. If both trigger, or if neither has triggered by the end of round 16, each team's value is its Interceptions minus its Miscommunications: the higher value wins and equal values are a draw. Both members of a team share its result.
variation.expected_effect: Both teams always have had the same number of encryptions and interception chances when the game is checked. Alternating the first mover each pair spreads the small advantage of seeing the other team's result first equally between the teams. Removing the 7-point structural edge should bring win rates for equal-skill teams near 50/50, with some draws. Fixed Encryptor/Guesser roles make every player's job unambiguous. The strategic core is unchanged: clue clearly enough for a partner but vaguely enough to survive a reader of the public history. Talk is left out because the two teams' interests are directly opposed and teammate talk would bypass the cluing that is the game.

balanced.evidence:
PAYOFFS. Each team has 4 tokens: Interceptions and Miscommunications for A and for B. A team wins at 2 Interceptions or when the other team reaches 2 Miscommunications. In any one round only the encrypting team can gain a Miscommunication and only the other team can gain an Interception. Both events push toward the same winner, so the stated 'cannot point to different winners in the same round' is arithmetically true. Every failure Team A suffers happens in odd rounds (A's Miscommunication or B's Interception), and every failure Team B suffers happens in even rounds.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES under the WINNER RULE.
- Decoder always submits 1-2-3, or any fixed code: correct 1/24 of the time, so the team gains a Miscommunication about 96% of rounds and loses by about its 2nd encryption. It loses against sensible play and against random play.
- Interceptor always submits a fixed code: hits 1/24 (4.2%) per round. That is about 0.29 expected hits over 7 attempts, so it essentially never reaches 2 Interceptions. A sensible interceptor reading the history beats it.
- Encryptor always writing the most obvious clue: the decoder is near 100% correct, but once history builds the interceptor's hit rate rises well above 1/24. This trades off; it does not dominate.
- Random play: 1/24 per decode, so it loses almost at once.
No option is strictly better, and no fixed policy avoids losing.

SEAT EDGE (the failure). Treat the game as a race in which each team fails with probability f per own encryption. Team A's failures arrive first (rounds 1, 3, 5, ...) and Team B's second (2, 4, 6, ...). A loses whenever N_A <= N_B, where N is the number of own turns needed to reach 2 failures. With f = 0.25 and P(n) = (n-1)f^2(1-f)^(n-2), the values are P(2)=.0625, P(3)=.094, P(4)=.105, P(5)=.105, P(6)=.099, P(7)=.089, P(8)=.078, P(9)=.067. The sum of P(n)^2 is about 0.063 plus a tail, giving P(tie in turns) of about 0.07. P(A loses) is about (1+0.07)/2, roughly 53.5% against 46.5%: a 7-point structural edge for Team B. Splitting failures into two separate counters makes equal-pace races more frequent, which widens the edge. The original Decrypto resolves both teams' clues in the same round before checking for a winner, so equal pace there is a tie, not a loss for the team that encrypts first. The variation removed that symmetry. Both teams can realistically win, but the seat order hands B a measurable advantage on every equal-pace race.

playable.evidence:
LIMITS. 13 steps (at most 20), 3 choice steps (clue, decode, intercept; at most 4), 16 attributes (at most 20), 3 hidden elements (A's keywords, B's keywords, the code; at most 3), 1 random draw per round (the code), 16 rounds (at most 40). All within limits. The clue-validity check is a complex rule ruled by the referee, which is allowed; scores and the winner are arithmetic on public token counts. The game is finite, with a 16-round cap and an Interceptions-minus-Miscommunications tiebreak. Decoder and interceptor guesses are a simultaneous poll, as required. Having no talk is sensible: the clues are the only intended channel, and teammate talk would bypass the cluing.

AMBIGUITY (the failure). The rules define the Interceptor as 'the member of the other team who is not that team's next Encryptor', then list a schedule that contradicts that definition in half the rounds:
- Round 5: B's next Encryptor is B1 (round 6), so the Interceptor should be B2; the list says B1.
- Round 13: same, should be B2; the list says B1.
- Round 7: B's next is B2 (round 8), so it should be B1; the list says B2. Round 15 is the same.
- Round 6: A's next is A1 (round 9), so it should be A2; the list says A1. Round 14 is the same.
- Round 8: A's next is A2 (round 11), so it should be A1; the list says A2. Round 16 is the same.
- Round 10: A's next is A2 (round 11), so it should be A1; the list says A2.
Rounds 1, 3, 9, 11 and the A-side rounds 4 and 12 agree. A model with only these words cannot tell who intercepts in rounds 5-8 and 13-16.

MINOR. Step 1 announces an Interceptor in rounds 1-2, where step 5 says there is none.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
CHANCE SOURCES. There are three: the code draw (uniform over 24), the keyword deal (some noun sets are easier to clue apart), and the referee's validity ruling.
- The code is shown to the Encryptor, and decoding depends on clue quality. A well-coordinated pair decodes about 90% or more of the time, against 4.2% by chance.
- Interception depends on mapping the public clue history to keyword columns. It is near chance in round 3 but rises sharply as columns fill. Each encryptor must judge each clue against what the opponent has already seen.

INFERENCE AND PLANNING. There is real inference: deducing the opponent's hidden keywords from accumulated clues, modelling what the partner will associate, and planning clues so they do not reveal the column themes. That is opponent modelling under hidden information with a direct way to act on it, through intercept guesses and clue choice.

WHEN BOTH TEAMS PLAY WELL. Decoding is near perfect, so the game is decided by interception skill and clue obscurity over many rounds, not by a single draw. The deal varies difficulty but good play overcomes it.

Estimated share of the result due to chance: about 20-30%, mainly the deal and early-round guessing, plus the seat edge noted under balanced. The better reasoner is clearly favoured.

required_changes: Balanced: make the two teams' rounds symmetric. Treat rounds 2k-1 and 2k as one pair and run the end check only after each even round, using the token totals after both teams have encrypted. If both teams meet a win condition in the same pair, decide by Interceptions minus Miscommunications, and declare a draw if equal. Remove the stated claim about same-round conflicts, or restate it for pairs.

Playable: replace the contradictory Interceptor list with one consistent schedule. Under the stated principle it is: R1 B2, R3 B1, R5 B2, R7 B1, R9 B2, R11 B1, R13 B2, R15 B1; R4 A1, R6 A2, R8 A1, R10 A1?? To avoid any derivation, simply state a fixed list and drop the principle. For example, Interceptor = the opponent who is NOT encrypting in the next round: R3 B1, R4 A1, R5 B2, R6 A2, R7 B1, R8 A2, R9 B2, R10 A1, R11 B1, R12 A1, R13 B2, R14 A2, R15 B1, R16 A2. Verify this list against the encryptor table before publishing.
Playable: in step 1, announce no Interceptor in rounds 1 and 2.

balanced.evidence:
Thoughtless policies, judged by the WINNER RULE.
(1) Decoder always submits 1-2-3, or any fixed code. P(correct) = 1/24, so P(Miscommunication) is about 0.958 per own encrypt. The team holds 2 Miscommunications after its first two encrypts in about 92% of games, so the opponent triggers by the end of pair 2. This policy LOSES almost always.
(2) Interceptor always submits a fixed code, or a random one. P(hit) = 1/24 per attempt. Over 7 attempts, P(at least 2 hits) = 1 - (23/24)^7 - 7(1/24)(23/24)^6, about 3.6%. Against a decoding opponent it does not win. Against a sensible interceptor it falls behind on Interceptions minus Miscommunications.
(3) Encryptor always gives the most obvious clue (a near-synonym). Decoding is close to 100%. Each keyword's column then becomes transparent after 1-2 appearances. An attentive interceptor can map clues to numbers, and an exact intercept of 1 in 24 codes becomes close to certain. The opponent reaches 2 Interceptions around pairs 3-4. This LOSES against sensible play.
(4) Encryptor always gives obscure clues. The own Decoder fails, which gives Miscommunications, so this LOSES.
No option is strictly better.
The intercept guess is free. Always submitting your best guess is the natural optimum, the same as in the original, and not a degenerate shortcut.

Payoff of the main tension, per encrypt:
| clue style | P(decode ok) | P(intercept) |
| obvious | ~1 | high after history |
| balanced | high | low |
| obscure | low | ~1/24 |
The trade-off is real.

Seat edge. Win checks happen only at the end of each pair, so order within a pair cannot settle a race. Odd pairs have A encrypt first and even pairs have B encrypt first, so the order alternates. When each side intercepts in pair p, its interceptor has seen the same number of the opponent's clue sets (p-1). Information is symmetric.
Roles rotate: A1 and B1 encrypt in odd pairs, A2 and B2 in even pairs. The role table matches the rule text in all 16 rounds.
Both teams can realistically win. The comparison at round 16 and the simultaneous-trigger tie-break are pure arithmetic.
